title: Finding Favourite Tuples on Data Streams with Provably Few Comparisons

problem.claim: Identify one or more high-utility tuples for a user with unknown preferences using as few adaptive pairwise comparisons as possible.

contributions.claim: A single-pass streaming algorithm processes each tuple at most once while keeping memory usage and requested comparisons logarithmic in the total number of tuples in the worst case.
The approach preserves its theoretical guarantees when users may declare ties between tuples with nearly equal utility.
The work enhances existing pruning techniques using mathematical programming tools.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report systematic evaluation on synthetic and real-life datasets, including scalability analysis.
The authors report superior performance over existing methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Finding high-utility tuples is difficult when user preferences are unknown.
Pairwise comparisons are used to elicit preferences, and the paper seeks to minimize the number of adaptive comparisons.
A single-pass streaming algorithm provides worst-case logarithmic memory and comparison requirements.
The guarantees extend to tie declarations, and mathematical programming strengthens existing pruning techniques.
The proposed algorithms are evaluated on synthetic and real-life datasets for scalability and comparison with existing methods.

source_observation.claim: The method adapts user comparisons while processing each stream tuple only once and maintaining logarithmic worst-case resource bounds.

interpretation.claim: Interactive preference elicitation can be combined with streaming constraints when the algorithm limits both retained state and requested feedback.

application.claim: This pattern may apply to large, continuously arriving collections where user feedback is costly and data cannot be revisited.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the preference model, comparison assumptions, or settings under which the guarantees apply.

unknowns: Formal algorithm details and proof arguments are not provided.
The preference model and comparison-noise assumptions are unspecified.
Dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, baselines, and quantitative results are unspecified.
